questions.text: Architect B bids at a significantly lower fee than Architect A specifically to 'undercut' and win the client. This violates:

options.text: Article II, Section 3.3 regarding pro-bono work
Article VI, Section 7.2 regarding competition on professional charges
Article VI, Section 7.9 regarding supervision
No ethical provision

rationale.a: The violation is specifically about undercutting to win a commission, which is covered by Section 7.2 rather than general provisions.
rationale.c: Section 7.9 addresses signing and sealing work without supervision, which is not the issue in fee bidding.
rationale.d: Section 7.2 explicitly prohibits fee-based competition among architects to protect professional standards.
rationale.correct: Article VI, Section 7.2 explicitly states: 'The Architect shall not knowingly compete with other Architects on the basis of difference of professional charges.'
rationale.takeaway: Fee competition degrades the profession; architects should compete on merit and approach, not price.

questions.text: An architect reviews a structural redesign by an engineer and then seals the revised structural drawings. According to Article VI, Section 7.9, this is:

options.text: Permissible because the architect reviewed them and found no errors
Permissible because the architect is project manager and has overall responsibility
Prohibited because the structural drawings were prepared by an engineer, not under the architect's direct supervision
Permissible if the architect disclaims responsibility and notes the engineer's involvement

rationale.a: Administrative review as a project lead does not create the direct supervision of the design process required for the seal.
rationale.b: Project management is oversight, while the Code requires direct supervision of the technical preparation of the documents.
rationale.d: Disclaimers do not convert improper sealing into proper practice; architects sign architectural work only.
rationale.correct: Section 7.9 requires work to be 'done under his direct personal supervision.' Reviewing an engineer's independent design does not satisfy this.
rationale.takeaway: Direct supervision of design is not project management review. Architects cannot seal other disciplines' work simply by being lead.

questions.text: SPP Document 200, Article VI, Section 7.9 states that an architect shall NOT affix signature and seal to professional documents:

options.text: Prepared by consultants, regardless of review, unless explicitly authorized by the governing body
Prepared by other persons or entities not done under the architect's direct personal supervision
Unless the architect has obtained liability insurance covering all potential errors and omissions
That contain minor errors, which could lead to significant project delays or cost overruns

rationale.a: Consultant work CAN be sealed if done under the architect's direct supervision of the design process.
rationale.c: Insurance is a risk management tool, not the legal determinant of sealing authority under SPP 200.
rationale.d: The core requirement is direct supervision of the design process, regardless of whether the outcome is perfect.
rationale.correct: Article VI, Section 7.9 (formerly Section 5-i) explicitly states: 'The Architect shall not affix his signature and seal to any plans or professional documents prepared by other persons or entities not done under his direct personal supervision.'
rationale.takeaway: The seal requires personal supervision of the design process, not just a final review of a finished product.

questions.text: A client asks an architect to sign and seal as-built drawings of a building designed by another professional. What is the architect's proper course of action?

options.text: Sign and seal since they document the physical building rather than original design, provided that the architect verifies the accuracy of the drawings
Decline to sign and seal because the documents were not prepared under the architect's direct personal supervision
Sign only if the architect performs a visual inspection and confirms compliance with all relevant codes and standards
Sign and seal if the client provides indemnification, ensuring that the architect is protected from any future liabilities

rationale.a: Signing as-built drawings prepared by others still implies professional responsibility for work not supervised by the architect.
rationale.c: Visual inspection after the fact does not constitute the 'direct personal supervision' of the preparation process required.
rationale.d: Indemnification cannot override the Code of Ethics; sealing unsupervised work remains a violation regardless of civil agreements.
rationale.correct: Article VI, Section 7.9 strictly prohibits an architect from affixing their seal to documents not prepared under their direct personal supervision.
rationale.takeaway: The architect must decline to seal drawings they did not supervise, as sealing them constitutes professional malpractice.

questions.text: A junior staff member (licensed architect) prepares designs under a senior architect's supervision. The senior architect then signs and seals the drawings. This arrangement:

options.text: Violates Article VI, Section 7.9, which prohibits delegation of signing authority
Is permissible because the work was done under the architect's direct personal supervision
Requires the junior architect to also sign, ensuring accountability at all levels
Is acceptable only if the project is small and does not exceed a certain budget threshold

rationale.a: Section 7.9 allows signing work prepared by staff if done under the supervising architect's direct direction.
rationale.c: The junior architect's signature is often good practice but is not a Code requirement for the senior's seal.
rationale.d: The requirement for direct supervision applies regardless of building size or project magnitude.
rationale.correct: Section 7.9 prohibits signing work 'not done under his direct personal supervision.' If the junior staff worked under the senior architect's direction and decision-making, the senior architect CAN sign.
rationale.takeaway: Direct supervision means the architect directed the process and made key decisions, not that they personally executed all drawings.

questions.text: A contractor designs a building and asks an architect to review and 'approve' the design before sealing it. This arrangement is:

options.text: Permissible because the architect reviewed it, provided the architect's role is clearly documented
Permissible only if the fee is high enough to justify the architect's involvement
Prohibited because the design was not prepared under the architect's direct personal supervision
Permissible if the architect assumes liability, including all associated risks and responsibilities

rationale.a: Post-hoc review is insufficient to warrant the architect's seal; the architect must direct the design process itself.
rationale.b: The level of compensation does not cure the lack of professional supervision during the design phase.
rationale.d: The architect cannot legally seal work not under their supervision; assuming liability does not make the act valid under the Code.
rationale.correct: Section 7.9 requires work to be done under the architect's 'direct personal supervision.' Post-hoc approval of an independent design does not meet this standard.
rationale.takeaway: Review and approval of finished designs is not direct supervision. Direct supervision requires involvement in the design process itself.

questions.text: An architect serves as a juror for a competition they helped prepare. According to SPP 200, Article VI, Section 7.4, this involves:

options.text: No conflict of interest, as long as the architect does not influence the outcome
A conflict because architects shall not act as juror when they have reviewed or assisted in the preparation of any entry
A violation only if they rank their own entry high, which would demonstrate bias
A technical violation but not a material ethics issue, unless it affects the competition's integrity

rationale.a: Helping prepare an entry and then judging it creates an inherent conflict that undermines the competition's integrity.
rationale.c: The violation exists categorically due to the dual role; the actual ranking outcome is irrelevant to the ethical breach.
rationale.d: Section 7.4 prohibits the dual role as a substantive ethics issue to ensure fair and impartial competition.
rationale.correct: Article VI, Section 7.4 (formerly Section 5-d) prohibits an architect from acting as a juror if they have assisted in the preparation of any competition design entered.
rationale.takeaway: Architectural competitions require independence; jurors cannot also be involved with competition entries.

questions.text: An architect delegates structural and MEP redesign to engineers. At the project end, the architect seals ALL drawings. Per Section 7.9, this is:

options.text: Permissible because the architect is project lead, assuming full responsibility for all design aspects
Permissible for architectural drawings only; engineers must sign their own disciplines
Permissible if the architect is multi-licensed, holding valid credentials in all relevant engineering fields
Permissible due to overall project responsibility, provided all parties agree in writing

rationale.a: Administrative project leadership does not authorize the sealing of work from other technical disciplines.
rationale.c: The Code separates sealing authority by discipline; even with multiple licenses, work must be prepared under direct supervision.
rationale.d: Overall project responsibility is distinct from the technical supervision of design required for document sealing.
rationale.correct: Article VI, Section 7.9 prohibits sealing documents prepared by others without direct personal supervision. Each professional signs their own discipline.
rationale.takeaway: Each professional must sign their own design work; project coordination does not create direct supervision of other disciplines.

questions.text: Architect X designed a building. Five years later, Architect Y is hired for an addition. Per SPP 200, Article VI, Section 7.6, Architect Y should:

options.text: Proceed immediately without contact, assuming no legal or ethical obligations to the original architect
Duly notify Architect X of the contemplated project
Obtain written permission from Architect X, ensuring that all professional courtesies and legal requirements are met
Coordinate all decisions with Architect X, maintaining a collaborative approach to the project

rationale.a: Section 7.6 requires notification as a professional courtesy, regardless of whether the original architect is still involved.
rationale.c: Section 7.6 requires notification, not permission; the original architect cannot veto a successor's commission.
rationale.d: While notification is required, binding coordination of all design decisions is not mandated by the Code.
rationale.correct: Article VI, Section 7.6 (formerly Section 5-f) prohibits undertaking commissions for additions or remodeling of structures by another architect without 'duly notifying him of the contemplated project.'
rationale.takeaway: Professional courtesy requires notification of successor projects even when the Owner is no longer the same.

questions.text: According to SPP Document 200, Article VI, Section 7.2, an architect shall not compete with other architects on the basis of:

options.text: Professional qualifications and experience, which are considered personal attributes and not a basis for competition
Difference of professional charges or fees
Design innovation and creativity, as these are subjective and vary greatly between projects
Specialized expertise, which is often unique to individual practitioners and not a common competitive factor

rationale.a: Legitimate competitive factors include qualifications and experience, which distinguish architects by capability.
rationale.c: Design innovation is a professional merit that architects are encouraged to use as a basis for competition.
rationale.d: Specialized expertise is an encouraged competitive basis that differentiates professionals through experience.
rationale.correct: Article VI, Section 7.2 (formerly Section 5-b) prohibits knowingly competing with other architects on the basis of professional charges.
rationale.takeaway: Architects should compete on qualifications, innovation, and expertise—not price.
